content: The physician-patient relationship is defined as the interactions between a physician and a patient. Patients expect their physicians to actively listen to them. A positive relationship between the physician and the patient is associated with better health outcomes. A systematic review of the medical interview process highlights several key practices for physicians: Prepare with intention by taking a moment to focus before greeting the patient. Listen intently and completely by sitting down, leaning forward, and avoiding interruptions. Agree on what matters most by identifying the patient’s priorities and incorporating them into the visit agenda. Connect with the patient’s story by considering life circumstances that influence their health, acknowledging their positive efforts, and celebrating their successes. Explore emotional cues by noticing, naming, and validating the patient’s emotions. A qualitative study identified eight attributes of effective healthcare providers: Pay attention to the small details. Take time with the patient. Be open and listen. Find something to like or love about the patient. Remove barriers to communication. Allow the patient to explain their concerns. Share authority in decision-making. Be committed to the patient’s care. Being an empathetic listener and adopting a caring, rather than dominant, attitude can enhance the physician-patient relationship. A supportive relationship characterized by warmth, attention, and confidence has been shown to reduce pain in conditions like irritable bowel syndrome. However, it remains unclear whether physicians should wear traditional attire during consultations. Before the interview, various methods to help patients prepare questions have been studied, but none have shown a strong effect. When greeting the patient, one study of videotaped physician-patient encounters suggested that physicians should shake hands with patients but remain sensitive to nonverbal cues that might indicate whether the patient is comfortable with this behavior. Regarding the use of names, it is recommended that physicians initially address patients by their first and last names and introduce themselves using their own first and last names. Collaborative agenda-setting at the start of the visit may reduce last-minute concerns raised by patients at the end of the visit. When hearing the patient’s story, physicians often interrupt patients before they finish listing their concerns, which occurs in about three-quarters of interviews. While it is unclear whether this interruption is harmful, failing to ask for the patient’s concerns at all may lead to additional concerns being raised later in the interview. After the patient states their primary concern, responding with “Is there something else you want to address in the visit today?” rather than “Is there anything else you want to address in the visit today?” may reduce the likelihood of unmet concerns. Encouraging patients to participate in decision-making can improve their engagement and compliance with treatment plans. Using stories to explain medical evidence may enhance communication. Patient activation can be measured using the Patient Activation Measure. Readiness to change can be assessed using tools like the Readiness to Change Ruler or the University of Rhode Island Change Assessment (URICA) questionnaire, which is based on the Transtheoretical Model of Change. The URICA includes 23 or 32 items, and a shorter 12-item version has been developed. The Ruler correlates with the full questionnaire and predicts behavioral intentions. Health literacy can be assessed to ensure patients understand their medical conditions and treatment plans. The length of the visit is often insufficient to address all patient concerns, despite the increasing duration of medical visits. A higher number of medical problems or concerns brought by the patient can interfere with the quality of care. Preventive care alone, if coordinated solely by the physician rather than delegated, requires more time than is typically available. Longer visits are associated with higher quality care and greater patient satisfaction. Time constraints, however, reduce physician satisfaction. There is significant variability in the length of visits, but patient visits should ideally last at least 20 minutes. Patients, as well as healthcare professionals, often struggle to recall details of the discussion during the visit. The presence of a computer and electronic health records during the interview changes the dynamics of the interaction. Most patients do not mind when physicians seek online information and do not expect them to appear all-knowing. The by-the-way syndrome refers to patients raising new concerns at the end of the interview. Starting the interview by carefully eliciting the patient’s agenda may help avoid this issue. However, when by-the-way concerns arise, they are often psychosocial in nature, while physicians tend to respond with biomedical solutions. Higher ratings of patient-provider communication are associated with increased adherence to preventive measures, such as regular mammography screenings. In general, communications between a patient and physician are privileged and cannot be disclosed in court proceedings. Exceptions exist for reporting certain contagious diseases, child abuse, and other specific events. Privileged information is protected under the Privacy Rule of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).
